RE: Formal Appeal of Adverse Benefit Determination
Member: Skyler Alvarez
Member ID: W485219153
Reference Number: POC-8B473A1D50-39674
Date of Notice: 2026-08-21
Requested Service/CPT: Rotator cuff repair, CPT 29827
Treating Surgeon: [Dr.] Reyes, MD, Orthopedic Surgery

To the Cigna Appeals Unit:

I am writing to formally appeal the denial described in the Notice of Adverse Benefit Determination dated 2026-08-21 (Reference No. POC-8B473A1D50-39674), which states that my request for arthroscopic rotator cuff repair (CPT 29827) is denied because, in the plan's words, "the imaging findings submitted do not support the medical necessity of the requested procedure." I am submitting this appeal within the 180-day window stated in the notice (deadline 2027-02-17).

1. The governing coverage policy

Based on my own review, the medical-necessity criteria Cigna applies to CPT 29827 are contained in the coverage policy titled "CMM-315: Shoulder Surgery - Arthroscopic and Open Procedures," a Comprehensive Musculoskeletal Management guideline developed by EviCore and administered for Cigna (Version 2.0.2025, effective March 7, 2026; publicly posted at https://www.evicore.com/sites/default/files/clinical-guidelines/2025-11/Cigna_CMM-315%20Shoulder%20Surg%20Arthro%20Open%20Proc_V2.0.2025_Eff03.07.2026_Pub11.21.2025.pdf). That document's table of contents confirms it contains dedicated sections titled "Rotator Cuff Repair Indications" (p. 26) and "Rotator Cuff Repair Non-Indications" (p. 28).

I was not able to obtain the full bulleted text of those two sections, and I want to be transparent about that: I am not quoting, paraphrasing as a quotation, or otherwise attributing specific bullet-point criteria from the "Rotator Cuff Repair Indications" section to Cigna or EviCore in this letter, because I do not have that verbatim text in hand. Under 29 C.F.R. §2560.503-1(g) and (j), I am entitled to receive, free of charge, the specific rule, guideline, protocol, or other similar criterion relied upon in denying this claim. I formally request that Cigna provide the complete text of the "Rotator Cuff Repair Indications" and "Rotator Cuff Repair Non-Indications" sections of CMM-315 (V2.0.2025), along with a written, itemized explanation of which specific criterion or criteria in that section the reviewer found unmet, so that I and my surgeon can respond point-by-point.

What I can confirm from the portions of CMM-315 I did review is the following, quoted directly from the document:

- "These guidelines apply to services or supplies managed by EviCore for Cigna as outlined by the Cigna CPT list."
- "The determination of medical necessity for the performance of shoulder surgery is always made on a case-by-case basis."
- From the policy's own definition of "Rotator Cuff Tear (RCT)": "Evaluation of rotator cuff muscle quality with CT or MRI is an important consideration. Chronic and larger tears are associated with muscle atrophy and fatty replacement, both of which correlate with inferior functional outcome after rotator cuff repair. It is thought that early repair of acute rotator cuff tears might mitigate the development of chronic tendon and muscle pathology and improve functional outcomes."
- The same definitions section classifies full-thickness ("complete") tears as follows: "Small: <1cm; Medium: 1-3cm; Large: 3-5cm; Massive: >5cm."

2. Why the submitted imaging and clinical record support medical necessity

Applying the above framework to my own records, submitted with the original prior authorization request:

- Imaging: MRI of the shoulder dated 2026-07-13 demonstrates a full-thickness supraspinatus tear measuring 1.8 cm — which, using the plan's own size classification quoted above, falls within the "Medium: 1-3cm" category of full-thickness tear — with grade 2 fatty atrophy. This is an objective, positive imaging finding of a structural rotator cuff tear, not an inconclusive or negative study.
- Chronicity/risk of delay: The plan's own guideline recognizes that "[c]hronic and larger tears are associated with muscle atrophy and fatty replacement, both of which correlate with inferior functional outcome after rotator cuff repair" and that timely repair "might mitigate the development of chronic tendon and muscle pathology and improve functional outcomes." My tear has already progressed to grade 2 fatty atrophy after 12 months of symptoms; further delay risks additional muscle quality loss and a worse surgical outcome.
- Symptom duration and functional loss: I have had progressive shoulder pain for approximately 12 months, unrelieved by rest. I am currently unable to lift my arm above shoulder height or sleep on the affected side — a significant, documented loss of shoulder function affecting activities of daily living.
- Physical examination: My exam findings include positive provocative testing on the affected side and range of motion limited by pain, consistent with the MRI-documented structural tear.
- Failed conservative management: I completed 14 weeks (16 visits) of supervised physical therapy focused on rotator cuff strengthening and scapular mechanics (2026-03-25 through 2026-07-01), as documented in the physical therapy discharge note; used NSAIDs for 8 months with inadequate relief; and received a corticosteroid injection on 2026-05-12 that produced only 3 weeks of partial relief before symptoms returned. This represents a substantial, well-documented trial and failure of provider-directed non-surgical management, not a rush to surgery.
- No disqualifying factors: There is no active infection, no untreated substance use disorder, and I am a non-smoker with a BMI of 29.

Given this record, the imaging did not fail to show pathology — it affirmatively demonstrates a full-thickness, medium-sized supraspinatus tear with early fatty atrophy, in a patient with 12 months of function-limiting symptoms who has already failed an extensive, guideline-consistent course of conservative care. I ask that Cigna's reviewing medical director re-examine the MRI report and full clinical file in light of these facts, consistent with the policy's own statement that "[t]he determination of medical necessity for the performance of shoulder surgery is always made on a case-by-case basis."

3. Requested action

I respectfully request that Cigna:
1. Reverse the denial and authorize CPT 29827 (arthroscopic rotator cuff repair) as medically necessary; or
2. If the denial is upheld, provide the complete, verbatim "Rotator Cuff Repair Indications" and "Rotator Cuff Repair Non-Indications" sections of CMM-315 (V2.0.2025) and identify in writing the specific criterion or criteria that my clinical file does not satisfy, so that my surgeon, Dr. Reyes, and I may respond or pursue further appeal, including independent external review, within the applicable timeframes.

Enclosed with this appeal are: the physical therapy discharge note (2026-03-25 to 2026-07-01, 16 visits); documentation of NSAID use and the 2026-05-12 corticosteroid injection and response; the MRI report dated 2026-07-13; office examination notes documenting positive provocative testing and pain-limited range of motion; and a supporting letter from Dr. Reyes. [Attach copies of all referenced records.]

Please confirm receipt of this appeal and advise of the expected decision date. I understand that pre-service medical-necessity appeals are generally decided within 30 calendar days. I can be reached at [phone number] or [email address], and my surgeon's office can be reached at [surgeon's office phone/fax] for any additional clinical information needed.

Sincerely,

Skyler Alvarez
